What do our country's symbols and holidays mean, and whose stories do they tell?
symbol. A picture or thing that stands for an idea. Example: a heart is a symbol for love.
liberty. Freedom. Being free to make your own choices.
holiday. A special day when people remember a person or event, or celebrate together.
monument. A statue or building made to help people remember someone or something.
tradition. Something a family or group does again and again, like a parade or a meal on a holiday.
emancipation. Setting people free from slavery.
proclamation. An official public message from a leader.
A symbol is a thing that stands for an idea. The United States flag is a symbol of our country. It has 13 stripes and 50 stars . Each part stands for something.

I ask: what does each part stand for? There are 13 stripes. The first 13 states began as 13 colonies. So the stripes stand for them. There are 50 stars. Today there are 50 states. So each star stands for one state. When a new state joined, a star was added.

Many people say Betsy Ross sewed the first flag. Is it true? A historian looks for proof. Betsy Ross was a real flag maker in Philadelphia. But her grandson, William Canby , first told this story in 1870 , almost 100 years later. No papers from 1776 show it. So we say: it is a famous story, but we are not sure it happened.
Liberty means freedom. The Liberty Bell is in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor. Both are symbols of freedom. But people have asked: freedom for whom?

Let me read the words on the bell: "Proclaim LIBERTY throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants thereof." That means: tell everyone in the land they are free. But in the 1830s, millions of people were still enslaved. People working to end slavery saw this. They named it the Liberty Bell . They made it a symbol of ending slavery.

Look at her feet. There are broken chains . Broken chains mean freedom. Look at her arm. She holds a tablet with the date July 4, 1776 . Look up high. Her torch lights the way. In 1903, a poem was put inside her base. It welcomes immigrants , people who come from other countries to live here.
A holiday is a special day to remember or celebrate. Every holiday tells a story. A historian asks: Whose story is it? Who is missing? The answers help us understand our country better.

Take July 4th . In 1776, leaders approved the Declaration of Independence. It said "all men are created equal." But many people were not free then. In 1852, Frederick Douglass gave a speech. He asked what July 4th meant to people who were still enslaved. One holiday can mean different things to different people.

The second Monday in October has two names. Many places call it Columbus Day . Many Italian Americans celebrate it with pride. Columbus arrived in the Americas in 1492. Then Columbus and his men forced Taíno people to work, and many died. So many places also celebrate Indigenous Peoples' Day . It honors the nations who were already here, and still are.

Part of the order: The people of Texas are informed that, in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all enslaved people are free. Note: we changed the words enslaved people. The order used an older word. Word help: informed means told. Executive means the President. Timeline: January 1, 1863: President Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation says enslaved people in the states fighting the Union are free. April 1865: The Civil War is ending. Few Union soldiers are in Texas. June 19, 1865: General Gordon Granger gives General Order Number 3 in Galveston, Texas. December 1865: The 13th Amendment ends slavery in the whole country. June 17, 2021: Juneteenth becomes a national holiday.

Opal Lee. Opal Lee grew up in Texas. When she was 12, an angry crowd forced her family out of their new home in Fort Worth. It happened on June 19, 1939. She became a teacher. At age 89, she began walking to ask leaders to make Juneteenth a national holiday. At each stop she walked 2.5 miles. The 2.5 miles stand for the 2.5 years Texas waited for the news. In 2021, she stood beside the President when Juneteenth became a holiday. She is called the Grandmother of Juneteenth . She turned 100 in 2026.

Frederick Douglass. Frederick Douglass was born enslaved in Maryland. In 1838, he escaped to freedom. He became a great speaker and writer against slavery. On July 5, 1852, he gave a famous speech in Rochester, New York . He asked what July 4th meant to people who were still enslaved.

Emma Lazarus. Emma Lazarus was a Jewish American poet from New York City. She helped Jewish immigrants who came from Russia . In 1883, she wrote a poem about the Statue of Liberty. It calls the statue the Mother of Exiles . In 1903, her poem was put on a plaque inside the statue's base.

Indigenous Peoples' Day organizers. In 1990, Indigenous leaders from across the Americas met in Quito, Ecuador . Soon it would be 500 years since 1492. They asked: why tell only Columbus's story? In 1992, the city of Berkeley, California , became one of the first places to celebrate Indigenous Peoples' Day. Today many states and cities celebrate it.
